explanations.explanation: That's the number, friend. John 5:5 says this man had been an invalid for thirty-eight years. That's a long stretch of years to live with that condition. Hold onto that number, because it makes what happens next hit even harder.

Twelve is a real stretch of time, but the text gives a much bigger number. The man had been an invalid for thirty-eight years (John 5:5). Twelve doesn't even get you to a third of that. So his condition had lasted far longer than you guessed.

Eighteen shows up in another story, a woman who had been crippled for eighteen years (Luke 13:11). But the man at Bethesda is a different person with a bigger number. John 5:5 says thirty-eight years. That's twenty more years than the number you picked.

explanations.answer: Do you want to get well
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. Jesus asks him, “Do you want to get well?” (John 5:6). After thirty-eight years, Jesus starts with a question instead of a speech. I think that's a kind way to begin a talk with someone who's been lying there so long.

explanations.answer: Do you believe I can do this
explanations.explanation: That's a real question Jesus asks, but He asks it to two blind men in another story (Matthew 9:28). Here at the pool, He asks the man something simpler: “Do you want to get well?” (John 5:6). No test of belief shows up in this scene. Just that one plain question.

explanations.answer: Why are you lying out here
explanations.explanation: Jesus doesn't ask why the man is there at all. John 5:6 says He saw him lying there and realized he had spent a long time in this condition. Then He asks, “Do you want to get well?” So Jesus already knew the situation and went straight to the heart of it.

explanations.answer: He has no one to help him in
explanations.explanation: That's it. He tells Jesus, “I have no one to help me into the pool when the water is stirred.” (John 5:7). He adds that while he is on his way, someone else goes in before him. I think there's a lot of weight in that answer.

explanations.answer: The guards keep him away from it
explanations.explanation: No guards in this scene. The man says he has no one to help him into the pool when the water is stirred. He also says that while he's on his way, someone else goes in before him (John 5:7). The trouble is that nobody is there to help him, and nobody mentions a guard.

explanations.answer: The priests say he is unclean
explanations.explanation: The man never mentions priests, and the text says nothing about anyone calling him unclean. His problem is simpler. He has no one to help him into the pool when the water is stirred, and while he is on his way, someone else goes in before him (John 5:7). That's all he says.

explanations.answer: Get up and pick up your mat and walk
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend! Jesus tells him, “Get up, pick up your mat, and walk.” (John 5:8). No pool, no waiting, no one racing him to the water. Jesus just speaks, and that's all it takes.

explanations.answer: Go and wash in the pool of Siloam
explanations.explanation: That one belongs to a different story, where Jesus tells a blind man to go wash in the pool of Siloam (John 9:7). At Bethesda, nobody gets sent to a pool at all. Jesus says, “Get up, pick up your mat, and walk.” (John 5:8). The pool isn't part of it.

explanations.answer: Go and show yourself to the priests
explanations.explanation: Jesus tells that to a man healed of leprosy in another story (Luke 5:14). Here He gives a different command: “Get up, pick up your mat, and walk.” (John 5:8). Three things to do, and none of them involve a priest. The man's mat comes along for the walk.
Not slowly, friend. John 5:9 says, “Immediately the man was made well…” He didn't need a few days of recovery or a slow climb back to his feet. He picked up his mat and began to walk, right then.
That's right. John 5:9 says, “Immediately the man was made well…” No waiting around and no gradual improvement. After thirty-eight years, he picked up his mat and began to walk.

Yes, carry. The Jews tell him, “This is the Sabbath! It is unlawful for you to carry your mat.” (John 5:10). They don't say a word about the miracle. They go straight to the mat. I'd have been asking, “Wait, how are you WALKING?”
Nobody mentions selling anything. The Jews tell the man it's the Sabbath and it's unlawful for him to carry his mat (John 5:10). He's just a man holding a mat. That's the whole complaint.
Washing isn't in this scene. What bothers them is that he's carrying his mat on the Sabbath. They say, “It is unlawful for you to carry your mat.” (John 5:10). Same mat Jesus told him to pick up.

That's the word. He answers, “The man who made me well told me, ‘Pick up your mat and walk.’…” (John 5:11). His point is simple: the man who made him well is the one who told him to do it. That's the answer he gives the Jews.

Seeing belongs to the blind men in other stories. This man had been an invalid, and the one who healed him told him to pick up his mat and walk. So he says, “The man who made me well told me, ‘Pick up your mat and walk.’…” (John 5:11). The word is well.

Hearing isn't what happened to this man. He had been an invalid, and Jesus made him well. He tells the Jews, “The man who made me well told me, ‘Pick up your mat and walk.’…” (John 5:11). Well is the missing word.

explanations.answer: Jesus had slipped away in the crowd
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. John 5:13 says the healed man did not know who it was, because Jesus had slipped away while the crowd was there. He got healed, and the one who healed him was already gone. I think that's a head-scratcher, and I've never been so quietly vanished on.

explanations.answer: Jesus told him to keep it quiet
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't report Jesus telling him to keep anything quiet. John 5:13 says the man did not know who it was, because Jesus had slipped away while the crowd was there. So the reason the text gives is that Jesus was gone.

explanations.answer: He forgot it in all the excitement
explanations.explanation: Forgetting isn't the reason the text gives. He didn't know who it was, because Jesus had slipped away while the crowd was there (John 5:13). I can't say what he felt in all that excitement. What the text says is that Jesus was already gone.

True. Jesus finds him at the temple and says, “See, you have been made well. Stop sinning, or something worse may happen to you.” (John 5:14). That's a serious word, and I think it's said with care. Jesus went and found him, and that matters.

It's actually true. John 5:14 says Jesus found the man at the temple and told him, “Stop sinning, or something worse may happen to you.” It's a heavy line, and the text doesn't say what the sin was. So we leave that open, just like the text does.

Not a secret, friend. John 5:15 says the man went away and told the Jews that it was Jesus who had made him well. Earlier he didn't know the name, and now he does. The text doesn't tell us why he told them, so I'll leave that where I found it.

That's right. John 5:15 says the man went away and told the Jews that it was Jesus who had made him well. When they asked him earlier, he did not know who it was (John 5:12-13). Now he names Jesus to the Jews.

explanations.answer: My Father is working and so am I
explanations.explanation: Yes! Jesus says, “To this very day My Father is at His work, and I too am working.” (John 5:17). He doesn't back up. He points to His Father and says He's working too. That sets up everything He says next.

explanations.answer: The Sabbath was made for man
explanations.explanation: Jesus says that in a different Sabbath moment, when He says the Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath (Mark 2:27). Here at Bethesda, He answers differently: “To this very day My Father is at His work, and I too am working.” (John 5:17). He ties His work to His Father's.

explanations.answer: I came to fulfill the Law
explanations.explanation: Jesus does say He came to fulfill the Law, but that's in the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5:17). Here He answers the Jews with, “To this very day My Father is at His work, and I too am working.” (John 5:17). Same Jesus, different moment.

There's a second reason, friend. John 5:18 says the Jews tried all the harder to kill Him because He was breaking the Sabbath, and also because He was calling God His own Father, making Himself equal with God. So the Sabbath wasn't the only thing. Good thing you can still see both.

That's right. John 5:18 says, “Not only was He breaking the Sabbath, but He was even calling God His own Father, making Himself equal with God.” Two things, and the text names both. The Sabbath was only part of it.

It's the other way around, friend. Jesus says, “…the Son can do nothing by Himself, unless He sees the Father doing it.” (John 5:19). He doesn't act apart from the Father. He goes on to say, “For whatever the Father does, the Son also does.”

Right. Jesus says, “…the Son can do nothing by Himself, unless He sees the Father doing it. For whatever the Father does, the Son also does.” (John 5:19). He's not working alone. The Father and the Son are doing the same work together.

True! Jesus says, “…just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom He wishes.” (John 5:21). Giving life to the dead is no small thing. That's a claim big enough to shake a chef's hat right off.

That one's actually true. John 5:21 says, “…just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom He wishes.” The Son gives life too, just like the Father does. It's a big claim, and Jesus makes it plainly.

explanations.answer: So all may honor the Son like the Father
explanations.explanation: Yes! Jesus says the Father has assigned all judgment to the Son “…so that all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father.” (John 5:22-23). Then He adds that whoever does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent Him. The two go together. You can't skip one and keep the other.

explanations.answer: So the Father can rest from His work
explanations.explanation: Rest isn't the reason. Jesus just said the Father is at His work to this very day (John 5:17). The reason in verse 23 is “…so that all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father.” Nothing there about the Father needing a break.

explanations.answer: So the Son can test the priests
explanations.explanation: Priests aren't mentioned in this part at all. Jesus says the Father has assigned all judgment to the Son “…so that all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father.” (John 5:23). That's the reason He gives. It's about honor, not a test.

Life! Jesus says whoever hears His word and believes Him who sent Him “…has eternal life and will not come under judgment. Indeed, he has crossed over from death to life.” (John 5:24). Crossed over, friend. Death on one side, life on the other.

Glory is a big word in this talk, but it's not the one here. Jesus says the person who hears and believes “…has crossed over from death to life.” (John 5:24). Glory shows up later, when Jesus talks about glory from men (John 5:41). Here it's life.
Rest isn't the word Jesus uses. He says the one who hears His word and believes “…has crossed over from death to life.” (John 5:24). Death on one side, life on the other. That's the crossing.

Not just the good ones, friend. Jesus says “all who are in their graves will hear His voice and come out” (John 5:28-29). Then He says those who have done good go to the resurrection of life, and those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment. The hearing isn't limited to the good ones.

That's right. Jesus says “all who are in their graves will hear His voice and come out” (John 5:28-29). Those who have done good come out to the resurrection of life, and those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment. Nobody gets left out of the hearing.

explanations.answer: He seeks the will of the One who sent Him
explanations.explanation: Yes. Jesus says, “…My judgment is just, because I do not seek My own will, but the will of Him who sent Me.” (John 5:30). He also says, “I judge only as I hear.” So His judgment rests on the will of the One who sent Him, not on His own will.

explanations.answer: He has studied every word of the Law
explanations.explanation: Jesus never gives that as His reason. He says His judgment is just “…because I do not seek My own will, but the will of Him who sent Me.” (John 5:30). It rests on the Father's will. Not on homework.

explanations.answer: The priests have approved His rulings
explanations.explanation: No priest signs off on anything here. Jesus says, “I judge only as I hear. And My judgment is just, because I do not seek My own will, but the will of Him who sent Me.” (John 5:30). The reason is the Father's will, plain and simple.

Jesus says the opposite, friend. He says, “There is another who testifies about Me, and I know that His testimony about Me is valid.” (John 5:32). The text doesn't name that person right there. Jesus just says there is one, and what He says next gives more witnesses.
That's right. Jesus says, “There is another who testifies about Me, and I know that His testimony about Me is valid.” (John 5:32). He isn't standing alone. And He's about to list who stands with Him.

explanations.answer: A lamp that burned and gave light
explanations.explanation: Yes! Jesus says, “John was a lamp that burned and gave light, and you were willing for a season to bask in his light.” (John 5:35). A lamp burns and gives light for others to see by. And He says they were willing to bask in it, for a season.

explanations.answer: A tree planted by the water
explanations.explanation: That picture is from Psalm 1, where a person who delights in the law of the LORD is like a tree planted by streams of water (Psalm 1:2-3). Jesus doesn't use it for John. He says, “John was a lamp that burned and gave light…” (John 5:35). It's all about light here.

explanations.answer: A city set on a hill
explanations.explanation: Jesus does use that image, but for His followers in the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5:14). For John, He picks something else: “John was a lamp that burned and gave light…” (John 5:35). A lamp, not a city.

explanations.answer: The works the Father gave Him to do
explanations.explanation: Yes! Jesus says, “the works that the Father has given Me to accomplish, the very works I am doing, testify about Me that the Father has sent Me” (John 5:36). The works speak. That includes the man who got up and walked at Bethesda.

explanations.answer: The crowds that follow Him around
explanations.explanation: Crowds aren't what Jesus points to. He says, “…the works that the Father has given Me to accomplish—the very works I am doing—testify about Me that the Father has sent Me.” (John 5:36). His testimony is His works. Not a crowd count.

explanations.answer: The praise of the temple priests
explanations.explanation: Jesus doesn't point to priests at all. He says His testimony is more substantial than John's because of the works the Father has given Him to accomplish (John 5:36). The works testify that the Father has sent Him. The priests aren't in the picture.

explanations.answer: Someone who comes in his own name
explanations.explanation: Yes. Jesus says, “I have come in My Father’s name, and you have not received Me; but if someone else comes in his own name, you will receive him.” (John 5:43). It's a sharp line. Jesus comes in the Father's name and isn't received, while someone coming in his own name would be.

explanations.answer: Someone who comes with signs from heaven
explanations.explanation: Signs from heaven aren't part of what Jesus says here. He says if someone else comes in his own name, they will receive him (John 5:43). That's the contrast. Jesus comes in His Father's name, and the other would come in his own.

explanations.answer: Someone the high priest sends to them
explanations.explanation: The high priest isn't mentioned here. Jesus says, “…if someone else comes in his own name, you will receive him.” (John 5:43). The key is the name. Jesus came in His Father's name, and this other one would come in his own.

Yes. Jesus says, “Your accuser is Moses, in whom you have put your hope.” (John 5:45). Moses, Israel's leader (Exodus 3:10), is the one they trusted. And Jesus goes on to say that Moses wrote about Him.

Abraham, Israel's forefather (Isaiah 51:2), is a big name, but he's not the one Jesus names here. Jesus says, “Your accuser is Moses, in whom you have put your hope.” (John 5:45). Moses was Israel's leader (Exodus 3:10), and the one they hoped in.

Elijah was a prophet (1 Kings 18:36), but Jesus doesn't name him here. He says, “Your accuser is Moses, in whom you have put your hope.” (John 5:45). Moses, Israel's leader (Exodus 3:10), is the one named. Jesus also says He Himself won't be the one accusing them.
